content: A national program is designed to provide both technical and managerial leadership to address tuberculosis (TB). The structure of these National TB Programs (NTPs) varies across countries. Some operate as dedicated standalone TB programs, while others are fully integrated within the Ministry of Health (MOH). In most cases, NTPs are managed under the MOH. Individuals affected by TB include those currently suffering from TB disease, those who have previously had TB, their caregivers, immediate family members, and members of key and vulnerable populations at risk for TB. Prioritization in TB care involves determining the relative importance or urgency of interventions. This process helps select strategies to address the most critical health needs identified through a situational analysis. It also involves deciding how to allocate often limited resources to implement the plan effectively. A programmatic gap refers to the difference between the current state of a TB program and its desired state, where it can fully meet its objectives. This includes gaps in TB service delivery to ensure universal access to quality care and gaps in management capacity to optimally coordinate the country’s TB response. The quality of care is defined as the extent to which health services—including promotion, prevention, treatment, rehabilitation, and palliative care—improve the likelihood of achieving desired health outcomes. These services must align with evidence-based professional knowledge while considering the needs and preferences of affected individuals and communities. A resilient health system is one that can prepare for and effectively respond to crises, maintain core functions during emergencies, and reorganize based on lessons learned. Such systems protect human life and ensure good health outcomes for all, even during and after crises. Social determinants of TB are non-medical factors that influence the disease and its outcomes. Examples include food security, housing, access to basic amenities, structural conflict, income levels, social protection, and access to affordable, quality health services. These determinants often have a greater impact on health than healthcare or lifestyle choices. TB comorbidity refers to the presence of another disease or health condition occurring simultaneously in a person with TB. The World Health Organization (WHO) published a toolkit in 2015 to assist countries in developing National Strategic Plans (NSPs) for TB. This guidance has since been updated to align with global commitments, strategies, and approaches. The updated document incorporates new tools, lessons learned, and approaches to TB programming and planning. The End TB Strategy, endorsed by the World Health Assembly in 2014, provides a strategic framework to achieve TB-related targets within the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). This includes ensuring universal health coverage (UHC) for all individuals affected by TB. Goal 3 of the SDGs focuses on ensuring healthy lives and promoting well-being for all ages. It includes targets to end epidemics of TB, AIDS, malaria, and neglected tropical diseases by 2030, as well as achieving UHC and access to quality essential health services. Goal 1 emphasizes ending poverty and achieving substantial social protection coverage for vulnerable populations. The 2018 UN High-Level Meeting on TB resulted in a political declaration committing to ambitious targets to end TB. This includes strengthening TB NSPs through multisectoral mechanisms and engaging civil society, affected communities, and stakeholders across and beyond the health sector. The 2018 Global Conference on Primary Health Care (PHC) led to the Declaration of Astana, which commits to bold political choices for health across all sectors. It envisions sustainable PHC systems that enhance resilience to prevent, detect, and respond to infectious diseases like TB, HIV, malaria, and hepatitis as part of UHC. The COVID-19 pandemic has destabilized the global economy and reversed progress in health and development, including TB care and prevention. Resources were redirected to the COVID-19 response, and public health measures restricting movement reduced access to TB services. This highlighted the need to maintain quality essential health services during emergencies. National strategic planning is essential to ensure that TB responses at the country level reflect changing contexts at national, regional, and global levels. An NSP provides medium-term direction for efforts to end TB, outlining goals, strategies, and prioritized interventions. It translates global and national commitments into actionable targets and activities, serving as a basis for mobilizing resources. Strategic planning for TB involves assessing the country’s situation, engaging stakeholders, and addressing TB through biomedical and social interventions. It also builds the capacity of affected communities and stakeholders to participate meaningfully in the TB response. The planning process must align with broader UHC and PHC agendas, reduce inequalities, and promote equity. Good practices for TB strategic planning include government stewardship, alignment with national health strategies, and multisectoral engagement. High-level leadership within the MOH ensures alignment with health priorities and facilitates stakeholder participation. The planning process should also address inequalities, protect human rights, and promote equity. The TB epidemic often disproportionately affects marginalized populations, who may face higher barriers to accessing services. Strategic planning must ensure that interventions are ethical, equitable, and responsive to the needs of these populations. It should also align with the national health strategy and other relevant programs to optimize synergies and resource mobilization. Effective stakeholder engagement is critical for the success of an NSP. This includes participation from government authorities, civil society, affected communities, and other stakeholders. Deliberate efforts should be made to engage these groups throughout the planning and implementation phases, ensuring that the NSP appropriately addresses the needs of those affected by TB.
